Right now on r/fitness: 16 year old girl diagnosed with scoliosis deadlifts 420 pounds. Shut the fuck up with your excuses fatties!

I think at 11 she was diagnosed with swole-iosis.

Solid

There's nothing wrong with it actually as long as her Doctor's are aware she's lifting.

I have a connective tissue disorder that also causes issues like kyphosis/scoliosis in many sufferers (myself included). Unfortunately I'm too far gone to safely lift any longer but it's actually recommended for many people with my kind of disorder!

It helps to slow the progression of major joint issues caused by the disease because all the extra muscle supports the weak joints.

As long as it's done properly (as in you're trained by someone that knows what they're doing and ensures you have proper form while lifting) then it's a really good way to exercise when you suffer from certain musculoskeletal issues.

I understand that people with an issue to muscle/skeleton/nerves have to work out to keep them in shape. I have a friend that suffers from (don't know English term) something that degenerates his nervous system. He HAS to work out/do a lot of cardio or risk becoming immobile. So he cycles 1h30 to college and 1h30 back (which, let's be honest, is overkill for any normal person) So I kinda understand working out to maintain your body when you are sick.

But scoliosis, an overcurved (bad) back, and then go deadlifting 420lbs (190kg)... at sixteen... As impressive as it is, it can't be beneficial.

Your spine should absorb the pressure while muscles absorb the tension. But your muscles are never able to absorb pressure. I understand that by lifting you increase your bone density. But, well, I'm skeptical it's enough of a positive influence to her condition. Deadlifting pressures the disks in between the spine as well, and those are not aligned in a person with scoliosis and thus are not bearing the load equally.

TLDR: I get it but think 420 is too much for a sixteen year old with scoliosis and think it will exacerbate rather than help.
